title: Resources a VM needs, and application hosting options
learningObjective: Describe the resources required to run a VM, and choose between web apps, containers and VMs to host an application.
foundation: A VM isn't one resource. It needs a size (CPU and memory), an image and OS disk, and networking: a virtual network with a subnet and a network interface (NIC).
Optional extras: a public IP address (to reach it from the internet), a network security group (firewall rules), data disks, and extensions.
To host an application you can use a web app (App Service), containers, or VMs. The more control you need, the more you manage.
engineer: Required: size (vCPUs, memory, temporary storage; changeable later), image (Marketplace or custom), OS disk (managed disk: Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, Ultra), virtual network and subnet, network interface.

Optional: public IP (Standard SKU is secure by default and needs an NSG rule to allow traffic), network security group, data disks, availability options, boot diagnostics storage, extensions (monitoring agents, scripts).
Each is a separate resource and some outlive the VM: deleting a VM doesn't delete its disks, NIC or public IP unless you chose 'delete with VM'. Leftover disks and IPs keep costing money.
Billing: compute is billed per second while running; a stopped (deallocated) VM stops compute charges but disks still cost.

Hosting options: Azure App Service (PaaS for web apps, REST APIs, background jobs; Windows or Linux; .NET, Java, Node.js, Python, PHP; deployment slots, autoscale, built-in authentication), containers (ACI, Container Apps, AKS), and VMs (full control, most management).
Choose App Service for standard web apps; containers for portable or microservice apps; VMs when you need OS access, custom software or legacy dependencies.

animation.caption: Build a VM from its required resources, then choose where to host each application.

example.title: Two apps, two choices
body: A marketing site built with Node.js goes on App Service: no VM to manage, staging slot for testing, autoscale.
A licensing server that needs a hardware dongle emulator and registry tweaks goes on a VM with a NIC, managed disk and an NSG allowing RDP from the office IP only.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription (a free account works)
permissions: Reader to explore; Contributor to create resources
portal: Create a VM: Basics (image, size), Disks (OS disk type), Networking (VNet, subnet, public IP, NSG), Management, Monitoring.
VM > Overview: see the linked disk, NIC and IP resources.
Create a resource > Web App: runtime stack and plan.
configuration.cli:
az vm create -g <rg> -n vm1 --image Ubuntu2404 --size Standard_B2s --vnet-name vnet1 --subnet default --public-ip-address "" --nsg-rule NONE --generate-ssh-keys
az webapp up -n <app> --runtime "PYTHON:3.12"

lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: Can't RDP to a new VM.
troubleshooting.cause: No public IP, or no NSG rule allowing 3389.
troubleshooting.fix: Use Bastion, or add a public IP and a rule limited to your IP.

troubleshooting.symptom: Costs continue after a VM was deleted.
troubleshooting.cause: Disks and public IPs were left behind.

comparisons.difference: App Service manages the OS and runtime; a VM gives full control and full responsibility.
Container Apps hides Kubernetes; AKS exposes it for full control.

misconceptions.myth: Stopping a VM in the OS stops billing.
A VM always needs a public IP.
misconceptions.reality: Private access via VPN or Bastion is safer.

architectureDecisions: Default to App Service for web apps.
Use VMs only when OS control is needed.
Avoid public IPs on VMs; use Bastion.
